paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: worship and listening belong together. The psalm opens with shouting and singing, then bows low before the LORD our Maker, the great King above all gods (Psalm 95:1-6). And the reason is simple: the depths of the earth, the mountain peaks and the sea are all His (Psalm 95:4-5). When the One you're singing to is THAT big, a joyful noise makes sense, friend, even if you sing like a squeaky oven door.

Then the psalm says we are "the people of His pasture, the sheep under His care," and turns to a warning: "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts" (Psalm 95:7-8). That's the part I want you to hold onto. God's people had seen His work, and they still tested Him, and God said of them, "They are a people whose hearts go astray, and they have not known My ways" (Psalm 95:9-10). Singing loud on a good day is the easy part, friend. The real question is what your heart does when God speaks.

The psalm ends with a heavy line, and I won't pretend it isn't: "They shall never enter My rest" (Psalm 95:11). I think it's there so we take "Today" seriously. So bring the song AND the listening ear, baker. Worship the Maker with your whole voice, then keep your heart soft enough to hear Him when He talks.
